title: Gemini 4 Neon for Revit and AutoCAD Teams: Reading a Pump Submittal
summary: See what Gemini 4 Neon’s Chartography score means for pump submittal review, then carry an approved equipment change into Revit or AutoCAD with ArchiLabs Desktop.
body_markdown:
Suppose a supplier offers to deliver a replacement chilled-water pump three weeks early. The new submittal still calls it P-2. The project manager wants to know whether the team can take the earlier delivery and keep the drawings they have.


The equipment schedule says what P-2 has to do. The supplier’s PDF shows what it can deliver and where the pipe connects. Gemini 4 Neon, which Google released on November 18, can read the spreadsheet alongside the PDF. Give it both and you can ask for the schedule row, the curve and the drawing for P-2 in one pass. Neon is available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app.[Google’s Gemini 4 Neon announcement](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-neon/)


## What the Gemini 4 Neon Chartography score tells a reviewer


Google reports that Neon scored **73.5% on Chartography** , a benchmark with 100 tasks built around charts professionals use at work. The original study records a familiar mistake. Models sometimes found the right part of a chart and still misread the value between two marks on an axis.[The Chartography research paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10677)


On a pump submittal, even the choice of line matters. One chart can show several curves, each for a different impeller diameter. Follow the neighboring line and you’ve just read the performance of a pump the supplier never offered.[ASHRAE’s guide to centrifugal pump curves](https://handbook.ashrae.org/handbooks/S24/IP/s24_ch44/s24_ch44_ip.aspx)


## How to use Gemini 4 Neon to review a pump submittal


Say P-2 calls for 120 US gallons per minute at 45 feet of head. Give Neon the schedule and the submittal and ask a question you can check with your finger on the page.


> Find P-2 in the schedule and the supplier’s selection sheet. What speed and impeller diameter is the supplier offering? On the curve for that selection, what head do you read at 120 US gpm? Give me the page and curve label, and flag any value you had to estimate.


Open the cited page, find 120 on the flow axis, and trace up to the selected curve. Read across to the head axis and compare it with the scheduled 45 feet. If the PDF doesn’t identify the impeller, you have a specific question for the supplier. Can they mark the curve for the pump they’re quoting?


## Updating the pump in Revit or AutoCAD with ArchiLabs Desktop


Once the engineer has approved the selection, the pipe still has to meet the flange. Take the supplier’s outline drawing and compare the inlet and discharge locations with the connections in the project. If the new inlet sits two inches higher, someone needs to know before the shop makes the connecting pipe.


Give that approved outline to ArchiLabs Desktop. In Revit, ask it to update the family type used by P-2, then open a section through the inlet to check the connection. In AutoCAD, ask it to revise the pump block and dimension the inlet from the top of the pad. You can watch Desktop build and place a native Revit equipment family from a manufacturer’s PDF.[Watch the ArchiLabs Desktop demo](https://archilabs.ai/desktop)


P-2 can do the job, but the drawing needs to change. With the two-inch offset marked, the project manager can send the detail to the shop and ask the question that decides whether those three weeks are worth taking. Has anyone cut that pipe yet?
